title: Graphs: Dijkstra's Shortest Path
oneLiner: BFS finds the shortest path by HOP COUNT; Dijkstra finds it by total WEIGHT, always finalizing whichever undiscovered node currently has the smallest known distance next.
keyTakeaway: BFS's queue works because every edge costs exactly 1, so "discovered earliest" and "closest" are the same thing -- once edges have different weights that's no longer true, so Dijkstra replaces the queue with a PRIORITY QUEUE ordered by current known distance, and always finalizes the closest undiscovered node next, relaxing (potentially shortening) its neighbors' distances every time a node is finalized.
explanation:
BFS (Graphs: BFS Traversal) finds shortest paths correctly only because every edge in an unweighted graph costs the same -- exactly 1 hop -- so processing nodes in the order they're DISCOVERED automatically processes them in order of distance too. The moment edges have different weights (a road network where some roads are longer than others, say), that guarantee breaks: a node discovered EARLY via an expensive edge might actually be farther away than a node discovered LATER via a cheap one.

Dijkstra's fix: replace BFS's plain queue with a PRIORITY QUEUE (a queue that always hands back the smallest item first, usually built on a heap) ordered by each node's current best-known distance from the source. Start with dist[source] = 0 and every other node at infinity. Repeatedly pop the closest not-yet-finalized node, mark it finalized, and RELAX every one of its edges -- for each neighbor, check whether going through the just-finalized node beats the neighbor's current best distance (dist[node] + edgeWeight < dist[neighbor]), updating it if so. Because the priority queue always hands back the globally closest remaining node, once a node is popped and finalized, its distance is guaranteed correct and permanent (this breaks down with NEGATIVE edge weights, which is exactly why Dijkstra requires non-negative weights and a different algorithm, like Bellman-Ford, handles negative ones).

The relaxation step is the one genuinely new idea beyond BFS: a node can be discovered MULTIPLE times with different candidate distances before it's finally popped and finalized, and only the smallest candidate that made it into the priority queue wins.

Watch the graph below run Dijkstra from node 0 -- each step finalizes the closest remaining node (green) and relaxes its edges, with every node's current best-known distance shown live.

starterCode.python:
def dijkstra(adjacency_list, source):
    # TODO: dist[i] = infinity for all i except dist[source] = 0. Use a min-heap of
    # (distance, node), starting with (0, source). While it's not empty, pop the
    # smallest; skip it if its distance no longer matches dist[node] (a stale entry).
    # Otherwise relax every neighbor: if dist[node] + weight < dist[neighbor], update it
    # and push (new_distance, neighbor). Return dist, using -1 for any node still at
    # infinity (unreachable) at the end.
    return [0] * len(adjacency_list)

Finalize node 3 (distance 8). No shorter distances found through it.
Finalize node 4 (distance 11). No shorter distances found through it.
Done -- every reachable node finalized. Shortest distances from 0: 0:0, 1:3, 2:1, 3:8, 4:11, 5:unreachable.

recognitionSignals: The problem is "shortest path" but edges have different costs/weights/distances -- if every edge weighs the same, plain BFS is simpler and sufficient.

All edge weights are non-negative. A negative edge weight anywhere means Dijkstra's "once finalized, never revisited" guarantee breaks -- that's a different algorithm's problem (Bellman-Ford), not this one.
gotchas: A node can sit in the priority queue with more than one candidate distance at once (an earlier, worse one and a later, better one) -- when the worse, STALE entry is eventually popped, it must be skipped rather than reprocessed, since the node's true shortest distance was already finalized by the better entry.

Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights. With a negative edge, a node already finalized (and "locked in") could later turn out to have a shorter path after all -- something Dijkstra's greedy finalize-and-never-revisit step can't handle.
confusableWith: Graphs: BFS Traversal (this track) is the special case of Dijkstra where every edge weighs exactly 1 -- BFS's plain queue is a priority queue that never needs actual re-prioritizing under those conditions.

complexity.note: Every successful relaxation pushes a new entry instead of updating the old one (lazy deletion), so there are at most E + 1 pushes and as many pops, with stale entries skipped when popped. The queue can hold up to E entries, so each push or pop is O(log E), and log E ≤ log V² = 2 log V, which makes it O(log V). Total O((V + E) log V), often written O(E log V) for a connected graph. Space: dist is O(V), and the queue can hold O(E) entries including stale ones, so O(V + E). (A plain array scan for the minimum instead gives O(V²) -- fine for dense graphs, slower for sparse ones.)
